items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
items.snippet: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

items.snippet: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
items.snippet: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

items.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
items.snippet: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

items.title: Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
items.snippet: Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.

items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
items.snippet: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

items.title: Fatty liver disease is actually five different conditions, scientists discover
items.snippet: A common liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide may be far more complicated than scientists previously realized. Mayo Clinic researchers have discovered that fatty liver disease actually consists of five distinct biological subtypes, each carrying different risks for liver failure, cancer, heart disease, and other serious complications.

items.title: How life on Earth experiences climate change

items.title: You Need to stop Using INCOGNITO Mode Right Now
items.snippet: Incognito Mode doesn’t make you anonymous online, and it may reveal far more about you than you think. When you open a private Chrome window, your browsing history and cookies are removed from your device after you close it. But that’s about where the privacy ends. Your IP address is still visible, your internet provider can still see which domains you visit, websites can still run tracking script
